items.question: What drew you to the potential of machine learning in computational biology?
items.object: Machine learning’s potential contribution to computational biology
items.answer: I was trained as a machine learning researcher. When I was a PhD student, I was working on the problem of dealing with high-dimensional data. At that time, when I was a PhD student at Stanford, in the field of computational biology there was something really exciting happening, something called microarray data. It's gene expression data that measures expression levels over 20,000 genes. I thought that if machine learning researchers developed powerful and effective methods to identify causes of diseases such as cancer and therapeutic targets for those diseases, then as a machine learning researcher I could contribute hugely to science and medicine. I just fell in love with this field. That's how I got into research at the intersection of machine learning and computational biology.

items.question: Why do you believe biology and medicine will merge in the future?
items.object: The future convergence of biology and medicine
items.answer: The goals of the fields are slightly different from each other, but in the future I strongly believe that those two fields will merge: biology and medicine. Clinical scientists and researchers are already generating biological, molecular biology data from patients. For example, for cancer patients, you can think about measuring gene expression levels or genetic data from those cancer patients. What you want is treatment: you want AI or machine learning models to tell you which treatment, which drug, which anti-cancer drugs are going to work the best for that particular patient. For that, you definitely need biology knowledge and actual mechanistic understanding of cancer.

items.question: How do you think researchers should be trained to advance work at the intersection of computer science, biology, and medicine?
items.object: Training researchers at the intersection of computer science, biology, and medicine
items.answer: I usually tell my students, or other young people, that to actually move the field forward, to advance biology, medicine, or biomedical sciences, you really need to become a bilingual researcher, or even trilingual these days: computer science plus biology plus medicine. You have one brain that really thinks like machine learning researchers and biologists and clinical experts. That really helps to come up with a creative approach that can move the field to benefit patients. At the end, the ultimate goal of biology and molecular biology is to understand life better so that you can advance the health of humans. Collaborations definitely help, but at the end we really need to think about how to produce young researchers so that they really think like experts in this area.

items.question: Why do you think off-the-shelf feature attribution methods are insufficient for explainable AI in biology?
items.object: Feature attribution and meaningful explainability in biology
items.answer:
The core part of explainable AI, at least this theoretical framework, basically means feature attributions. Imagine you have a black box model, a set of input, a vector X, and an output Y. When you have a prediction, you want to find a way to attribute it to a feature, so you want to know which features contributed the most. There are mathematical frameworks, and our particular approach, called the SHAP framework, is based on game theory. That's the core of the technical side of explainable AI.

On the other hand, if you just apply an explainable AI technique, an off-the-shelf explainable AI algorithm, to biology, mostly it's useless. It's not very useful in terms of biological insight. What you really want to understand is how these features collaborate with each other. Imagine you have a set of genes as features. We have 20,000 genes; 20,000 expression levels are the input of the black box model, and your prediction is which cancer drug is going to work the best for each patient. Individual genes' contributions and gene importance scores by themselves are not going to be really useful. It will only be useful when an explainable AI algorithm can tell you which pathway, how genes collaborate with each other, how genetic factors play a role in that, and how that leads to good prognosis for the cancer patient and responsiveness to that drug. There is something missing there. The uniqueness of my research is that we want to develop explainable AI methods for biology and clinical medicine such that they can make a real, meaningful contribution to these fields.

items.question: How do you think counterfactual images help you understand a melanoma classifier's reasoning?
items.object: Counterfactual explanations for melanoma image classifiers
items.answer: Another example on the medicine side: imagine you have a deep model, a neural network, that's going to take a dermatology image. Say you find something unusual on your skin and take a picture. That's your dermatological image, and let's say you want to know whether that has features of a melanoma or not. The prediction result itself is not going to be really useful. Sometimes even the current explainable AI methods that tell you which pixels, which parts of the images led to the prediction of melanoma or not, are not going to be very useful to understand how this black box model really works. When you modify the image and generate a counterfactual, small changes to the image such that it changes the prediction—for example, from melanoma to normal—only then you can understand how this model works, what the reasoning process of this black box machine learning model is like. Those examples I'm going to show.

items.question: How do you see explainable AI opening new research directions in biology and health care?
items.object: Explainable AI's potential in biology and health care
items.answer: Even explainable AI or feature attribution methods as is can be useful. I'm going to show many examples like that in both biology and medicine. In the second part of the talk I'm going to show how explainable AI can even open new research directions, specifically for biology and health care. Those examples I showed you, the systems-level insights or this kind of counterfactual image generation, can facilitate collaboration with humans, in this case a clinical expert. Part of the second part will be a deep dive into our recent paper to highlight how explainable AI can help cancer medicine design, cancer therapy design: basically how to choose the two chemotherapy drugs that's going to have a synergy for a particular patient. That's the paper that was recently published in Nature Biomedical Engineering.

items.question: Why do you consider a unifying understanding of feature attribution methods useful for advancing explainable AI?
items.object: A unifying principle for feature attribution methods
items.answer: One is principled understanding of current explainable AI methods, specifically feature attribution methods. For example, in one work we showed that our feature attribution method, SHAP, published in NeurIPS in 2017, unifies a large portion of the explainable AI literature, and 25 methods follow the exact same principle: explaining by removing features. It turned out that 25 feature attribution methods widely used in machine learning applications all go by the same principle. You assess the importance of each feature by removing them or removing subsets of them. That helps us understand what goes on, for example, when they fail, and improve and develop new explainable AI methods. I'm going to introduce a couple of unifying frameworks. This is about principled understanding of feature attribution methods.

items.question: How do you approach making SHAP computation practical while preserving its theoretical properties?
items.object: Making SHAP computation feasible
items.answer: On the computational side, we have explored many avenues to make SHAP computation feasible and faster. SHAP stands for Shapley Additive Explanations. That's it because they chose the third letter. That's the first author's choice, my student's choice, and I love the name. Computing Shapley values is theoretically very well supported, but computation-wise it's not really easy to compute; it involves exponential computation. We need to develop approximation methods such that we can compute them in a feasible manner. We developed many fast statistical estimation approaches, and you want to make sure that they have convergence and all the theoretically desirable properties are there. We also developed approaches for specific model types, for example ensemble tree models and neural networks. We have Deep SHAP and Tree SHAP, and more recently we also have a vision Transformer SHAP, a way to compute Shapley values for vision Transformers. There is another one called Fast SHAP. One way to make SHAP computation more feasible is to focus on specific aspects of models. For example, tree ensembles or neural networks have particular model types; there is a way to make this computation faster.

items.question: How do you think about adversarial robustness in model explanations?
items.object: Robustness of feature attributions to adversarial attacks
items.answer: More recently we also started to understand the robustness of the SHAP value to adversarial attacks. A few years ago, researchers in machine learning tried to understand how robust the machine learning model prediction results are toward adversarial attacks, and now we are looking into this issue in terms of model explanations, how robust feature attributions are. In our most recent paper we basically showed the removal-based approaches, including SHAP—earlier I said many feature attribution methods turned out to have the same principle, explaining by removal—those methods are more robust to this kind of adversarial attacks.

items.question: Why do you still prefer removal-based approaches such as SHAP for explaining models despite their computational demands?
items.object: SHAP and removal-based approaches to model explanation
items.answer:
We believe in this removal-based approach and cooperative game theory, and it has desirable properties. In our many experiments we still see that removal-based approaches are more robust, as I said, to adversarial attacks. In terms of various evaluation criteria, we still think those methods are more robust than the other class, which we characterized as propagation-based or gradient-based approaches. We still prefer removal-based approaches.

On the other hand, those approaches are computationally very intensive. The way SHAP works is basically that you try all subsets of features, add a feature of interest, check the model output, and average across all subsets of features. As you can imagine, it's computationally very intensive. When we now think about foundational or larger language models, these are really large models with a lot of parameters, and in a neural network gradient computation is perhaps easier than trying all sorts of sets of features. Practically, it's not as easy as the other class in terms of actual computation, but we still want to make this computation more feasible. We aim to develop clever approaches to reduce the computation and still maintain the desirable theoretical properties that this removal-based approach, or SHAP in particular, has.

items.question: Why do you see model explanations as especially valuable for choosing cancer drug combinations in your acute myeloid leukemia research?
items.object: Model explanations for discovering principles of cancer drug synergy
items.answer:
We chose AML as an example application. In general the cutting edge in the treatment of cancers such as AML has increasingly become combination therapy. The rationale here is that by choosing drugs that target complementary biological pathways, we can achieve greater anti-cancer efficacy. Basically, you choose two or three chemotherapy drugs and use them together so that they have synergy. Usually there is very good anti-cancer efficacy.

The issue is that choosing optimal combinations of drugs is a really hard problem. There are about hundreds of individual FDA-approved anti-cancer drugs, which means there will be tens of thousands of possible combinations when you consider pairwise combinations, and there could be even more if you consider non-FDA-approved experimental drugs in development or a combination of more than two drugs. Finally, different patients, even patients who have the same type of cancer, may respond differently to the exact same drugs because of their individual genomic characteristics.

Let's formulate this problem as a machine learning problem. You take this AML patient's gene expression levels. You get the blood of the patient and purify the cells so you have only cancer cells, and say you measure expression levels over 20,000 genes. Mathematically this is a 20,000-dimensional vector. Also, let's say you consider a pair of drugs, drugs A and B, and use various information about the drugs, for example the structure of these drugs or their biological targets. There are many datasets that can tell you that information, and you take those as machine learning input and want to predict the synergy between drugs A and B.

In this kind of problem, as I said, there will be tens of thousands of pairwise combinations of those drugs. In this situation, not only the prediction but also explanations will be extremely important. You want to be able to say that drugs A and B are going to work well, are going to have synergy together, because patient X has gene expression levels of A, B, and C high, or expression levels of a certain biological pathway are high. You need a set of explanations to do that. More importantly, if you think about all pairs of drugs, if there is an underlying principle in terms of when two drugs are likely to have synergy, then it's going to be even more useful.

What we did in this paper was get the explanations. We computed SHAP values for many combinations of drugs from the machine learning model, analyzed that, and identified the unifying principle in terms of when any pair of drugs A and B have synergy. We identified the pathway. It is called the stemness pathway. It is also called the hematopoietic stem cell-like signature. Cancers are sometimes more differentiated or less differentiated. Usually less differentiated cancers have a worse prognosis than more differentiated cancers. We identified this pathway that's really relevant to this stemness pathway, stemness is a mechanism, and found the underlying principle, which basically says that two drugs, one targeting less differentiated and the other targeting more differentiated cancer, are likely to work the best.

items.question: How do you view the choice of acute myeloid leukemia as the cancer type for your explainable AI approach to drug synergy?
items.object: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) as an application of explainable AI to cancer drug synergy
items.answer: AML is just one example. This kind of principle can be applied to many datasets. Computational biologists often need to work on the problem where the data are available. As you can imagine, blood cancer tissues are relatively easier to obtain compared to other kinds of tissues, so there are many available datasets, and also measurement of drug synergy from many samples. We happened to choose this cancer type because of data availability, but this approach can be broadly applicable to other types of cancer.

items.question: How do you understand what a biological pathway represents and what it means for it to be activated?
items.object: Biological pathways and pathway activation
items.answer: In the field of computational biology, first of all, pathway is not unique to disease. When we say pathway databases, it basically tells you the members of the genes in a pathway. That's it. Many sets of genes are also sometimes called gene sets. It doesn't depend on the disease. The way we view it is that it's not like all genes need to be activated for the pathway to be activated. We would expect only a subset of genes to be highly expressed to say that pathway is activated.

items.question: How do you think methods for extracting biological insights from large datasets should use prior knowledge?
items.object: The role of prior biological knowledge in computational methods
items.answer: It's extremely important for computational biologists, when we develop a method like this to get biological insights from large-scale datasets, to make sure that it does not fully depend on any sort of prior knowledge. The algorithm needs to be flexible. That's of key importance. In this particular example, we didn't use a pathway from the beginning. When the model training happens, we used genes as individual features, analyzed the feature attributions, and did the statistical test.

items.question: Why do you see feature correlation as a challenge for using SHAP values in biomedical datasets?
items.object: Feature correlation as a limitation of SHAP values in biomedical datasets
items.answer: Another challenge we ran into in that project was not really addressed properly by the foundational AI field: feature correlation. In many biomedical datasets you will see lots of features that are correlated with each other. Many genes are correlated; it's a really modular gene expression, so you easily see subsets of genes that are very highly correlated with each other. In that kind of case, SHAP values are not going to be extremely accurate, because imagine there are two genes perfectly correlated with each other. There will be infinite ways to attribute to these two genes. In that Nature Biomedical Engineering paper we addressed it by considering ensemble models.

items.question: Why are you interested in sample-based explanations of large language models and foundation models?
items.object: Sample-based explanations of large language models and foundation models
items.answer: We are really interested in sample-based importance. Say that you transpose the matrix, transpose your feature matrix. I've been talking about feature attributions a lot, but you can also apply Shapley values to gain insights into which samples are important for your model training. That can help us understand how foundational models in various fields or larger language models rely on which training samples. That can be really important from a model auditing perspective, first of all, and to gain insight into which samples were important for these large models to behave a certain way. Sample-based explanation is also one of the things that we are mainly working on.

items.question: What do you see as the central interpretability challenge in building foundation models for single-cell biological data?
items.object: Biologically interpretable foundation models for single-cell data
items.answer:
Single-cell data science is one of the big themes in my lab now. You obtain gene expression levels or other kinds of molecular-level information at a single-cell level. items.question: How do you assess the role of explainable AI in auditing clinical dermatology models?
items.object: Explainable AI methods for auditing clinical dermatology models
items.answer:
On the clinical side, we are really interested in model auditing. In our most recent paper, that's in review, we are focusing on a dermatology example. A dermatological image is inputted into the neural network, and you want to know whether the prediction result is melanoma or not. There are many algorithms out there, some published in very high-profile medical journals and some available through cell phone apps. There are many algorithms. We recently tested them with separate held-out test samples and got a result that's a little concerning in terms of usage. Our analysis showed that explainable AI was extremely helpful. For example, in the skin image, which part of the image led to that kind of prediction, or using counterfactual image generation: you make small changes to the input dermatology image such that it crosses the decision boundary of the classifier, and see what features were changing. That way you can see the reasoning process of this classifier, this clinical AI model.

For that there needs to be some technological development, because feature attributions themselves are not going to be enough. They show only a very small part of the inner workings of the machine learning model. Developing methods for auditing clinical AI models is another research area we are currently pursuing.

items.question: Why are you interested in sample-based explanations for large language models and other foundation models?
items.object: Sample-based explanations of large language models and foundation models
items.answer: We are really interested in sample-based importance. Say that you transpose the matrix, transpose your feature matrix. I've been talking about feature attributions a lot, but you can also apply Shapley values to gain insights into which samples are important for your model training. That can help us understand how foundational models in various fields or larger language models rely on which training samples. That can be really important from a model auditing perspective, first of all, and to gain insight into which samples were important for these large models to behave a certain way. Sample-based explanation is also one of the things that we are mainly working on.
